DCARL: A Divide-and-Conquer Framework for Autoregressive Long-Trajectory Video Generation

Junyi Ouyang Affiliation: Institute for Creative Technologies Affiliation: University of Southern California E-mail {junyiouy, wenbinte, gonglinc}@usc.edu, zhao@ict.usc.edu, chw9308@hotmail.com    Wenbin Teng Affiliation: Institute for Creative Technologies Affiliation: University of Southern California E-mail {junyiouy, wenbinte, gonglinc}@usc.edu, zhao@ict.usc.edu, chw9308@hotmail.com    Gonglin Chen Affiliation: Institute for Creative Technologies Affiliation: University of Southern California E-mail {junyiouy, wenbinte, gonglinc}@usc.edu, zhao@ict.usc.edu, chw9308@hotmail.com    Yajie Zhao Affiliation: Institute for Creative Technologies Affiliation: University of Southern California E-mail {junyiouy, wenbinte, gonglinc}@usc.edu, zhao@ict.usc.edu, chw9308@hotmail.com    Haiwei Chen Affiliation: Institute for Creative Technologies Affiliation: University of Southern California E-mail {junyiouy, wenbinte, gonglinc}@usc.edu, zhao@ict.usc.edu, chw9308@hotmail.com
Abstract

Long-trajectory video generation is a crucial yet challenging task for world modeling, primarily due to the limited scalability of existing video diffusion models (VDMs). Autoregressive models, while offering infinite rollout, suffer from visual drift and poor controllability. To address these issues, we propose DCARL, a novel divide-and-conquer, autoregressive framework that effectively combines the structural stability of the divide-and-conquer scheme with the high-fidelity generation of VDMs. Our approach first employs a dedicated Keyframe Generator trained without temporal compression to establish long-range, globally consistent structural anchors. Subsequently, an Interpolation Generator synthesizes the dense frames in an autoregressive manner with overlapping segments, utilizing the keyframes for global context and a single clean preceding frame for local coherence. Trained on a large-scale internet long trajectory video dataset, our method achieves superior performance in both visual quality (lower FID and FVD) and camera adherence (lower ATE and ARE) compared to state-of-the-art autoregressive and divide-and-conquer baselines, demonstrating stable and high-fidelity generation for long trajectory videos up to 32 seconds in length. Project page: https://junyiouy.github.io/projects/dcarl/

Keywords: 
Long-trajectory video generation, Video diffusion models, Controllable video synthesis

1 Introduction

Long trajectory video generation has emerged as a pivotal research direction in recent years [7, 34, 23, 6, 8, 28, 19]. Developing generative models that can simulate large-scale, realistic scenes is of paramount importance for terrain reconstruction, autonomous driving systems and world models. To achieve this, existing methods [9, 10, 1, 33] typically leverage video diffusion models (VDMs) to facilitate high-fidelity generation. However, while these models perform well on room-sized scenes, they scale poorly to the synthesis of extended sequences (e.g., 30-second videos). This is primarily because predicting the entire sequence collectively incurs a prohibitive computational cost, limiting their effectiveness for long-duration and large-scene tasks.

Autoregressive (AR) diffusion models [3, 15, 13] introduce causal attention mechanisms to VDMs, enabling long-sequence rollout through sliding-window inference and sophisticated noise scheduling. However, these models often suffer from severe drift due to exposure bias—a phenomenon arising from the discrepancy between training on ground-truth contexts and inferring from self-generated frames [35, 23]. These compounding prediction errors not only degrade visual quality but also severely compromise the effectiveness of external control signals like camera poses. As the synthesized content deviates from the valid manifold, the model increasingly loses its ability to interpret and adhere to the geometric constraints provided by the control trajectory. This decoupling creates a fundamental misalignment between the intended camera instructions and the actual synthesized motion, ultimately causing purely AR methods to fail in maintaining trajectory consistency over long trajectories.

Existing methods seek to alleviate exposure bias by mitigating the training–inference mismatch. Diffusion Forcing [3, 20] injects random Gaussian noise into conditional inputs, while Self Forcing [13] trains causal models on self-generated rollouts to narrow the distribution gap. Although these strategies mitigate local drifting, they fail to explicitly bound error propagation, leaving the challenge of stable frame quality and precise camera control on long trajectories largely unaddressed. Furthermore, techniques [32, 17] that incorporate attention sinks [26] can further impede controllability; fixed sink frames often introduce sink collapse [4] and severely hinder the model’s responsiveness to dynamic pose instructions, ultimately degrading camera motion fidelity and scene transitions across extended trajectories.

Therefore, in this work, we propose DCARL, a novel framework that utilizes VDM in an autoregressive norm. Our method follows a divide-and-conquer scheme, employing dual generators specifically tailored for the synthesis of global keyframes and local dense frames. Our key insight is that purely autoregressive generation inherently suffers from unbounded error accumulation. To overcome this, our framework first employs a full-sequence generator to jointly synthesize sparse keyframes across entire video timeline. By modeling these global keyframes jointly rather than sequentially, we effectively bypass autoregressive error propagation, establishing structurally accurate and semantic-consistent anchors for the entire long sequence.

Building upon these global anchors, our dense frame generator synthesizes the intermediate video segments via a constrained interpolation process. Specifically, the local generation is conditioned on both the surrounding keyframes, which serve as fixed constraints, and the preceding dense segment. We identify two failure modes in keyframe-interpolation-based video generation. First, the model can become overly anchored to the provided keyframes, resulting in keyframe duplication in their temporal neighborhood rather than synthesizing smooth, physically plausible motion, which yields unnatural dynamics. The second is boundary inconsistency, where the video exhibits abrupt transitions at segment boundaries. To address these issues, we propose Motion-Inductive Noisy Conditioning and a Seamless Boundary Consistency module, enabling more dynamic and natural long-video generation. As validated by our empirical results, our modeling of global keyframe anchors and local transitions achieves highly stable generation of high-fidelity, long trajectory videos with precise camera control. Notably, our approach successfully mitigates the severe visual drifts lie in existing autoregressive approaches, enabling controllable long trajectory video generation.

2 Related Works

Autoregressive Video Generation. Autoregressive video generation models synthesize a long sequence in a causal manner by predicting the next frame (or block) conditioned on past generated content. Therefore, they naturally support streaming output and long-horizon rollout, but they also amplify exposure bias, error accumulation, and long-context constraints. Recent works [3, 20, 13, 5, 17, 37] focuses on training-time forcing or rollout alignment to reduce the train–test mismatch. They replace purely teacher-forced learning with varying degrees of self-conditioned rollouts, aiming to make the training distribution closer to inference and thereby suppress drift over long trajectories. A second line of works [32, 30, 31] targets inference-time long-context stabilization and efficiency without, or with minimal, retraining. Although these methods achieve high-fidelity video generation and precise motion control, they fall short in long horizon scene generation task as the rapid scene changes increase extra challenges for pure autoregressive generation.

Long Horizon Scene Generation. Long-horizon scene generation targets temporally consistent, controllable rollouts that remain plausible over hundreds to thousands of frames, where the core challenges are compounding drift, long-context scaling, and multi-view consistency. One line of work extends diffusion world models to make long rollouts more stable and controllable: VISTA [8] and GAIA [19] emphasize richer conditional interfaces and design choices that better preserve structure across iterative sampling, while Epona [34] explicitly frames long-horizon synthesis as autoregressive diffusion and trains the model to tolerate its own rollout errors. A second family pursues drift-bounding objectives for interactive generation: LIVE [12] constrains long-term deviation through consistency-style training signals, aiming to prevent unbounded error accumulation without relying solely on teacher forcing.

3 Preliminary

Autoregressive Generation. Long-horizon video generation is typically formulated as an iterative factorization of the joint distribution conditioned on the control signals 𝒞\mathcal{C}:

p⁡(𝒱|𝒞)=∏i=1Sp⁡(Si|S<i,𝒞),p(\mathcal{V}|\mathcal{C})=\prod_{i=1}^{S}p(S_{i}|S_{<i},\mathcal{C}), (1)

where the sequence 𝒱\mathcal{V} is partitioned into SS contiguous blocks {S1,…,SS}\{S_{1},\dots,S_{S}\} of size BB. This unified formulation encompasses various granularities of generation depending on the choice of BB: token-level AR where BB represents sub-frame units such as spatial-temporal patches, frame-level AR where B=1B=1 for sequential frame-wise rollout, and segment-level AR where B>1B>1 for simultaneous synthesis of multiple frames.

Architecturally, these paradigms employ intra-block bidirectional attention for temporal correlation and inter-block causal dependency for scalability. While a larger block size BB improves generation quality and consistency by expanding the bidirectional receptive field, it increases training overhead in memory and computation, necessitating a balanced design for scalable long-video synthesis.

Divide-and-Conquer Paradigm. An alternative strategy for long-video synthesis involves a hierarchical decomposition of the generation task into global structural planning and local detail refinement. This paradigm is typically formulated by introducing a sparse structural proxy 𝒦\mathcal{K}, such as keyframes or semantic layouts, which abstracts the temporal evolution of the sequence:

p⁡(𝒱|𝒞)=p⁡(𝒦|𝒞)​p​(𝒱|𝒦,𝒞).p(\mathcal{V}|\mathcal{C})=p(\mathcal{K}|\mathcal{C})p(\mathcal{V}|\mathcal{K},\mathcal{C}). (2)

Establishing the global trajectory via 𝒦\mathcal{K} transforms dense synthesis into a constrained interpolation task. This hierarchy bounds prediction errors within structural anchors, preventing the unbounded drift typical of autoregressive rollout. While decoupling long-range structure from local synthesis enables scalable generation, the paradigm remains sensitive to the noise inherent in the structural proxy 𝒦\mathcal{K} and requires high-fidelity conditional mapping in p⁡(𝒱|𝒦,𝒞)p(\mathcal{V}|\mathcal{K},\mathcal{C}) to maintain overall consistency.

4 Methods

4.1 Overview

We define the task of long-trajectory scene generation as generating a dense video sequence 𝒱={I1,I2,…,IN}\mathcal{V}=\{I_{1},I_{2},\dots,I_{N}\} of length NN, conditioned on an initial frame I0I_{0} and a sequence of control signals (e.g., camera poses) 𝒯={c1,c2,…,cN}\mathcal{T}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{N}\}. The goal is to model the conditional distribution p⁡(𝒱|I0,𝒯)p(\mathcal{V}|I_{0},\mathcal{T}).

As illustrated in Fig. 2, our framework follows a two-stage divide-and-conquer pipeline. In the first stage, the keyframe generator GKG_{K} synthesizes a sparse keyframe set 𝒦={Ik1,…,IkM}\mathcal{K}=\{I_{k_{1}},\dots,I_{k_{M}}\} conditioned on the initial image I0I_{0}, camera trajectory 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and caption 𝒞\mathcal{C}. These keyframes establish the overall structural evolution of the video. In the second stage, the interpolation generator GIG_{I} synthesizes the dense sequence 𝒱\mathcal{V} in a segment-wise manner.

Following the autoregressive paradigm, GIG_{I} synthesizes each segment SiS_{i} by generating its constituent frames simultaneously. The generation is conditioned on a selected subset of keyframes {Iki,…,Ikj}\{I_{k_{i}},\dots,I_{k_{j}}\} and a history of pp previously generated frames {Iti∗−p,…,Iti∗−1}\{I_{t_{i}^{*}-p},\dots,I_{t_{i}^{*}-1}\} with ti∗t_{i}^{*} being the first frame index of the current segment. This design decouples global structural planning from local detail interpolation, effectively reducing cumulative drift while maintaining precise adherence to the given trajectory.

4.2 Keyframe Generation

The keyframe generator GKG_{K} generates the keyframe set 𝒦\mathcal{K} as defined in  Sec. 4.1. Specifically, we implement this mapping through a DiT-based[18] flow matching process ΦK\Phi_{K}:

𝒦=𝒟⁡(ΦK​(ϵ∣ℰ⁡(I0),𝒫,𝒞)),\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{D}\big(\Phi_{K}(\epsilon\mid\mathcal{E}(I_{0}),\mathcal{P},\mathcal{C})\big), (3)

where ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) is the initial Gaussian noise. Here, ℰ\mathcal{E} and 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the VAE encoder and decoder, and 𝒫={ck1,…,ckM}\mathcal{P}=\{c_{k_{1}},\dots,c_{k_{M}}\} represents the sampled poses from the global trajectory 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Our insight is generating keyframes would achieve bounded or mitigated error accumulation as illustrated by the following proposition:

Proposition 1 (Temporal Degradation via Perturbation Analysis)

Let et=It−It∗e_{t}=I_{t}-I_{t}^{*} denote the cumulative generation error at frame tt, where ItI_{t} and It∗I_{t}^{*} are the generated and ground-truth frames. Modeling the autoregressive (AR) generation as It+1=ℱ⁡(It,ϵt)I_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(I_{t},\epsilon_{t}), where ℱ\mathcal{F} is the generator mapping and ϵt\epsilon_{t} is the sampling noise. Assuming ℱ\mathcal{F} is LL-Lipschitz continuous with respect to the state (L=sup‖∇Iℱ‖≥1L=\sup\|\nabla_{I}\mathcal{F}\|\geq 1), a first-order perturbation analysis yields the cumulative error bound ‖eNb​a​s​e‖≤∑j=1NLN−j​‖ηj‖\|e_{N}^{base}\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{N}L^{N-j}\|\eta_{j}\|, where ηj\eta_{j} represents the local injection error at step jj. If ‖ηj‖\|\eta_{j}\| is bounded by a constant η\eta, this cumulative error diverges at least linearly 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) (and exponentially if L>1L>1). Our divide-and-conquer strategy mitigates this via keyframe anchoring; the interpolation error at any frame ‖eto​u​r​s‖\|e_{t}^{ours}\| is bounded by the convex combination of its anchoring keyframe errors plus a local constant.

Please refer to the supplementary material for complete proof. To ensure structural integrity and control precision, we incorporate the following designs:

Spatial-Structural Preservation. Standard temporal VAEs typically employ temporal compression, which is inherently lossy and degrades visual quality for sparse sequences with significant spatial displacement. To circumvent this, we treat the MM keyframes as a batch of independent images by reshaping the frame dimension into the batch dimension during encoding and decoding. This ensures that each generated keyframe maintains full spatial fidelity, providing a reliable foundation for subsequent interpolation.

Keyframe Sampling Strategy. We construct the structural skeleton by sampling keyframes from the sequence using a temporal stride Δ​k\Delta k. To ensure robustness across diverse motion scales, Δ​k\Delta k is randomly drawn from a discrete set of candidate strides during training. During testing, a constant stride Δ​ktest\Delta k_{\text{test}} is maintained. The selection of Δ​ktest\Delta k_{\text{test}} serves as a critical hyperparameter that modulates the trade-off between the computational efficiency of the keyframe generation process and the precision of the structural guidance provided to the interpolation model.

4.3 Interpolation Generation

The interpolation generator GIG_{I} synthesizes the dense video sequence 𝒱\mathcal{V} in a segment-wise manner. Specifically, for each segment SiS_{i}, we construct an input latent sequence 𝐳i​n\mathbf{z}_{in} by concatenating the noise with temporal context. The DiT-based flow matching process ΦI\Phi_{I} is formulated as:

Si\displaystyle S_{i} =GI​(ℋi,𝒦i,𝒯i,𝒞)\displaystyle=G_{I}(\mathcal{H}_{i},\mathcal{K}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{C}) (4)
=𝒟⁡(ΦI​(𝐳i​n,𝒯i,𝒞)),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}\big(\Phi_{I}(\mathbf{z}_{in},\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{C})\big),

where 𝐳i​n=[ϵ,𝐳ℋi,𝐳𝒦i]\mathbf{z}_{in}=[\epsilon,\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{H}_{i}},\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{K}_{i}}] represents the sequence formed by concatenating the initial Gaussian noise ϵ\epsilon, the encoded history 𝐳ℋi=ℰ⁡(ℋi)\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{H}_{i}}=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{H}_{i}), and the selected keyframes 𝐳𝒦i=ℰ⁡(𝒦i)\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{K}_{i}}=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{K}_{i}) along the temporal dimension.

Keyframe Selection Policy. For each segment Si={Iti∗,…,Itj∗}S_{i}=\{I_{t_{i}^{*}},\dots,I_{t_{j}^{*}}\} and the corresponding trajectory 𝒯i={cti∗,…,ctj∗}\mathcal{T}_{i}=\{c_{t_{i}^{*}},\dots,c_{t_{j}^{*}}\} in the interpolation stage, we select a local subset of keyframes 𝒦i⊂𝒦\mathcal{K}_{i}\subset\mathcal{K} to provide temporal context. This subset encompasses all keyframes within the segment’s temporal span, along with the nearest keyframes that immediately precede and follow the segment:

𝒦i={Ik∈𝒦∣kp​r​e≤k≤kn​e​x​t},\mathcal{K}_{i}=\{I_{k}\in\mathcal{K}\mid k_{pre}\leq k\leq k_{next}\}, (5)

where kp​r​e=maxk:Ik∈𝒦,k<ti∗kk_{pre}=\max_{k:I_{k}\in\mathcal{K},k<t_{i}^{*}}k and kn​e​x​t=mink:Ik∈𝒦,k>tj∗kk_{next}=\min_{k:I_{k}\in\mathcal{K},k>t_{j}^{*}}k. This policy ensures that each segment is synthesized with both look-back and look-ahead structural constraints, preventing trajectory drift at the segment boundaries.

Autoregressive Rollout. To synthesize long-trajectory videos, GIG_{I} operates via a sliding window. During each sampling step of the denoising process, the noisy latent 𝐳\mathbf{z} (which originates from ϵ\epsilon) is continuously updated while being anchored by the fixed historical tokens 𝐳ℋi\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{H}_{i}} and global keyframe tokens 𝐳𝒦i\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{K}_{i}} within 𝐳i​n\mathbf{z}_{in}. This hybrid conditioning allows the model to leverage both local continuity and global anchors in a unified attention space, which effectively mitigates exposure bias and error accumulation compared to purely autoregressive methods, while maintaining superior adherence to the camera trajectory 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i}.

Motion-Inductive Noisy Conditioning. A common failure mode in interpolation is keyframe duplication, where the model replicates pixels from keyframes instead of synthesizing motion. This identity mapping shortcut occurs because clean keyframes 𝐳𝒦i\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{K}_{i}} allow the model to minimize training loss by anchoring to visual guides rather than learning complex temporal transitions, leading to stuttering or unnatural transitions. To mitigate this, we perturb the keyframe latents with a consistent noise level during both training and inference:

𝐳~𝒦i=αc​𝐳𝒦i+σc​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈),\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathcal{K}_{i}}=\alpha_{c}\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{K}_{i}}+\sigma_{c}\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), (6)

where the coefficients αc\alpha_{c} and σc\sigma_{c} are hyperparameters that control the keyframe guidance and the noise intensity, respectively. This perturbation breaks the pixel-level shortcut, forcing ΦI\Phi_{I} to prioritize underlying motion dynamics and trajectory adherence.

Seamless Boundary Consistency. To eliminate visual fractures at segment junctions, we implement a latent substitution strategy consistently during training and inference. Specifically, we define a pp-frame overlap between segments and replace the first pp latents of segment SiS_{i} with historical latents 𝐳ℋi\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{H}_{i}} at each denoising step τ\tau. To ensure generalization to these deterministic boundaries, 𝐳ℋi\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{H}_{i}} is kept noise-free during ΦI\Phi_{I} training. By bridging the distribution gap, this design enforces strict continuity and prevents flickering or motion jumps, ensuring a seamless temporal flow across all segment boundaries.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experiments Setup

Implementation Details. Our model is built upon the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [22] architecture. We integrate camera control by adding camera feature maps to visual tokens within each DiT block, following the ReCamMaster [1] design. Both keyframe and interpolation generators are trained for 30,000 steps using the AdamW optimizer (LR: 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay: 0.01, β\beta: (0.9, 0.95)) with an effective batch size of 16 across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

We process a 480-hour subset of the OpenDV-YouTube (ODV-YT) dataset [29], segmented into 1-minute clips at 10 fps. Camera poses are reconstructed using π3\pi_{3} [24] every 0.5 seconds, with intermediate frames recovered via spherical linear and linear interpolation. Semantic scene descriptions are generated by Qwen2.5-Omni [27] from frames sampled at 20-second intervals.

For keyframe generation, the model is trained with |K|=21|K|=21 and temporal strides Δ​k∈{4,8,16}\Delta k\in\{4,8,16\}, while Δ​ktest=8\Delta k_{\text{test}}=8 is fixed during inference. For the interpolation stage, the number of conditioning keyframes |K||K| is randomly sampled from [1,10][1,10] during training. In the inference phase, we apply Motion-Inductive Noisy Conditioning with αc=0.7\alpha_{c}=0.7, σc=0.3\sigma_{c}=0.3, and set the boundary overlap to p=1p=1. Please refer to the supplementary material for further details.

Baselines. We compare our method with Diffusion Forcing (DiffF) [3], Self Forcing(SelfF) [13], Deep Forcing(DeepF) [32], Vista [8] and Stable Virtual Camera (SEVA) [36]. All models are finetuned for fair comparison.

Datasets. To evaluate the capability of generating videos across large spatial spans and maintain structural integrity in expansive static scenes, we conduct experiments on two large-scale datasets: the ODV-YT validation set and the nuScenes [2] validation set for zero-shot testing. All experiments are conducted on 150 sequences.

Evaluation Metrics. For video quality, we use Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [11] and Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [21] as primary metrics, reporting both overall and per-segment scores to assess stability. For camera control accuracy, we utilize π3\pi_{3} [24] to extract 6-DoF camera poses and report Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Absolute Rotation Error (ARE) after alignment. For segment continuity, we further use Motion Smoothness (MS) [14], PSNR and SSIM [25] to evaluate the discrepancy between adjacent generated segments.

5.2 Comparison on Long Trajectory Generation.

In Fig. 3, Tab. 1, and Tab. 2, we present qualitative and quantitative comparisons. While autoregressive baseline methods can generate reasonable short-term results, they suffer from severe error accumulation and temporal drifting as the video length increases. Notably, even with the incorporation of specialized strategies designed to mitigate drifting, these methods still exhibit sharp performance degradation on extended sequences. In contrast, our divide-and-conquer autoregressive design leverages global keyframes as structural anchors to ensure both long-range visual stability and effective camera control. This advantage is further demonstrated by our robust zero-shot generalization to unseen environments. When evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, our approach consistently maintains high generation quality and precise path adherence, significantly surpassing baseline methods without requiring additional fine-tuning. Besides, our method outperform SEVA in terms of camera controllability and video quality. Quantitatively, these results confirm that our framework remains remarkably stable across the entire horizon, providing superior performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. For more visualization results, please refer to the supplementary material.

5.3 Ablation Study

Keyframe Spatial-Structural Preservation. We compare our image-level encoding with a temporal compression baseline to evaluate its necessity for sparse keyframe generation. Results are calculated using the generated keyframe sequences for 16-second videos on ODV-YT. As shown in Tab. 3 and Fig. 4, applying temporal compression to keyframes with large spatial spans leads to significant performance drops. Specifically, the spatial displacement between distant keyframes makes the VAE’s 4:1 temporal compression inherently lossy, which severely degrades quality (higher FID). Furthermore, such compression obscures fine-grained geometric cues, hindering the camera encoder from learning precise representations, as evidenced by the elevated ATE and ARE.

Keyframe Sampling Strides. We investigate the impact of sampling strategies by varying the generation stride Δ​kg​e​n\Delta k_{gen} and interpolation stride Δ​ki​n​t\Delta k_{int} on 16-second ODV-YT video generation. Specifically, keyframes are initially synthesized at a stride of Δ​kg​e​n\Delta k_{gen} and subsequently filtered to the interpolation stride Δ​ki​n​t\Delta k_{int} to serve as conditioning anchors for the dense synthesis stage. As shown in Tab. 4, Δ​kg​e​n\Delta k_{gen} is the primary determinant of both visual quality and trajectory fidelity. Increasing Δ​kg​e​n\Delta k_{gen} from 4 to 16 consistently enhances the quality of structural anchors, which directly improves the final FID and FVD. In contrast, the interpolation stride Δ​ki​n​t\Delta k_{int} exerts a negligible influence on the overall performance. Regarding trajectory adherence, we find that neither excessively dense nor sparse generation is optimal for ATE and ARE; the former introduces redundant constraints that hinder motion naturalness, while the latter provides insufficient guidance to bound drift. Our balanced configuration of (8,8)(8,8) achieves the optimal trade-off between structural stability and generative quality.

Motion-Inductive Noisy Conditioning. Conditioning the interpolation model on noisy keyframes is essential for high-quality synthesis, as discussed in Sec. 4.3. We evaluate this in Tab. 5 and Fig. 5 on 16-second ODV-YT sequences. Quantitatively, we observe that while FID remains relatively stable, the FVD significantly deteriorates when noise is not consistently applied during both training and inference. Qualitative results in Fig. 5 reveal two distinct artifact patterns: (1) unnatural transitions, such as fade-like blending between keyframes, and (2) motion stagnation, where the model replicates imperfect conditioning keyframes. These temporal artifacts—which involve mode collapse where the model copies pixels rather than learning motion dynamics—explain why the FVD increases sharply despite the stable FID. This confirms that joint noisy training and inference forces the model to bypass "copy-paste" shortcuts and achieve smoother, more realistic video generation.

Seamless Boundary Consistency. We evaluate the segment consistency mechanism by providing Ground-Truth (GT) frames as boundary conditions and comparing generated frames proximal to the segment junctions against these targets. As shown in Tab. 6 and Fig. 6, simple segment overlap (Overlap) fails to guarantee visual coherence; the final frame of a preceding segment often deviates from the required starting pose of the subsequent one, resulting in noticeable motion and temporal fractures. While naively replacing the first frame with the preceding segment’s last latent (+Sub) ensures junction continuity, it introduces pronounced artifacts. This stems from a distribution mismatch where the model, expecting noisy inputs, struggles to process a clean and deterministic conditioning frame without explicit consistency training. In contrast, our full strategy (+Sub+Train) effectively bridges this gap, achieving superior smoothness and structural fidelity at segment junctions.

Necessity of Keyframe Anchoring. We evaluate the necessity of structural anchors by removing keyframe conditioning during the interpolation stage. Quantitatively, Tab. 7 shows that without keyframe guidance, the model suffers from long-term drifting and poor camera accuracy, with FID/FVD increasing sharply as the sequence extends and ATE/ARE being significantly worse. This confirms that keyframes are essential for bounding accumulated errors over long durations. Qualitatively, Fig. 7 illustrates that the unguided variant fails to maintain camera control during complex maneuvers, such as a left turn followed by a straight trajectory, resulting in noticeable scene distortion and path deviation. In contrast, our full model leverages keyframe anchors to ensure both visual stability and precise trajectory adherence across the entire 32-second horizon.

6 Conclusion and Future Works

In this paper, we presented DCARL, a divide-and-conquer framework that reformulates long-trajectory video generation through an autoregressive modeling paradigm. By decoupling the complex synthesis task into global structural planning via keyframe anchors and local refinement via segment-wise interpolation, our approach effectively bounds the cumulative drift inherent in traditional autoregressive methods. Extensive experiments on the large-scale OpenDV-YouTube and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that DCARL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance in both visual fidelity and trajectory adherence. Notably, our framework enables the stable synthesis of high-quality long trajectories for extended horizons up to 32 seconds, significantly surpassing existing baselines.

While our dual-generator design ensures stability, a promising direction is to investigate unified architectures that can jointly model the distribution of sparse keyframes and dense sequences within a single latent space without compromising generation quality.

Appendix

Overview. In this supplementary material, we first provide a detailed proof of Proposition 1 from the main paper in Section A. We then present additional implementation details in Section B, followed by additional results and analysis in Section C. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our work in Section D.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 1

We evaluate the generation quality using the Mean Squared Error (MSE), defined as MSE​(et)=𝔼⁡[‖et‖2]=‖𝔼⁡[et]‖2+Tr​(Cov​(et))\text{MSE}(e_{t})=\mathbb{E}[\|e_{t}\|^{2}]=\|\mathbb{E}[e_{t}]\|^{2}+\text{Tr}(\text{Cov}(e_{t})), where ‖𝔼⁡[et]‖2\|\mathbb{E}[e_{t}]\|^{2} represents the squared systematic bias (drift) and Tr​(Cov​(et))\text{Tr}(\text{Cov}(e_{t})) represents the error variance.

Part I: Statistical Divergence of Pure Autoregressive Generation

In pure AR generation, It+1=ℱ⁡(It,ϵt)I_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(I_{t},\epsilon_{t}), where ItI_{t} is the generated frame and ϵt\epsilon_{t} is the sampling noise. We analyze the stability by considering the cumulative error et=It−It∗e_{t}=I_{t}-I_{t}^{*}, where It∗I_{t}^{*} is the ground-truth frame. Using a first-order perturbation, we add and subtract ℱ⁡(It∗,ϵt)\mathcal{F}(I_{t}^{*},\epsilon_{t}) to decompose the error:

et+1\displaystyle e_{t+1} =[ℱ⁡(It,ϵt)−ℱ⁡(It∗,ϵt)]+[ℱ⁡(It∗,ϵt)−It+1∗]\displaystyle=[\mathcal{F}(I_{t},\epsilon_{t})-\mathcal{F}(I_{t}^{*},\epsilon_{t})]+[\mathcal{F}(I_{t}^{*},\epsilon_{t})-I_{t+1}^{*}]
≈∇It∗ℱ⋅et+ηt+1,\displaystyle\approx\nabla_{I_{t}^{*}}\mathcal{F}\cdot e_{t}+\eta_{t+1}, (7)

where ηt+1\eta_{t+1} is the single-step drift when conditioned on ground truth. Assuming ℱ\mathcal{F} is LL-Lipschitz with L=sup‖∇It∗ℱ‖L=\sup\|\nabla_{I_{t}^{*}}\mathcal{F}\|, we obtain the recursive norm bound ‖et+1‖≤L​‖et‖+‖ηt+1‖\|e_{t+1}\|\leq L\|e_{t}\|+\|\eta_{t+1}\|.

Proof (Derivation of AR Divergence)

Divergence Upper Bound. Unrolling the recursive inequality ‖et‖≤L​‖et−1‖+‖ηt‖\|e_{t}\|\leq L\|e_{t-1}\|+\|\eta_{t}\| from t=1t=1 to NN, with ‖e0‖=0\|e_{0}\|=0, we have:

‖e1‖\displaystyle\|e_{1}\| ≤‖η1‖\displaystyle\leq\|\eta_{1}\|
‖e2‖\displaystyle\|e_{2}\| ≤L​‖e1‖+‖η2‖≤L​‖η1‖+‖η2‖\displaystyle\leq L\|e_{1}\|+\|\eta_{2}\|\leq L\|\eta_{1}\|+\|\eta_{2}\|
…\displaystyle\dots
‖eNbase‖\displaystyle\|e_{N}^{\text{base}}\| ≤∑t=1NLN−t​‖ηt‖.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{N}L^{N-t}\|\eta_{t}\|. (8)

This formula reveals the catastrophic accumulation of error in pure AR models:

  • •

    Case L=1L=1: Assuming ‖ηj‖≤η\|\eta_{j}\|\leq\eta, the bound simplifies to ‖eN‖≤∑j=1Nη=𝒪⁡(N)\|e_{N}\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{N}\eta=\mathcal{O}(N), representing a linear growth of error norm bound.

  • •

    Case L>1L>1: The geometric series diverges as 𝒪⁡(LN)\mathcal{O}(L^{N}), where local artifacts are exponentially amplified.

Divergence Lower Bound. While the Lipschitz upper bound describes the maximum potential error, the intrinsic divergence of pure AR generation is governed by the persistent nature of single-step errors ηt\eta_{t}. In practice, the learned mapping ℱ\mathcal{F} is subject to exposure bias, where the distribution gap between training and inference leads to a non-vanishing systematic drift. We formally assume that the expected single-step error is bounded away from zero, i.e., ‖𝔼⁡[ηt]‖≥μ>0\|\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t}]\|\geq\mu>0, or potentially increases with tt as the state ItI_{t} departs from the training distribution.

Furthermore, to prevent visual signal decay over time, the mapping ℱ\mathcal{F} must be non-contractive, meaning it does not shrink the latent state space in any direction. Formally, we assume the minimum singular value (the smallest scaling factor) of the Jacobian 𝐉t=∇It∗ℱ\mathbf{J}_{t}=\nabla_{I_{t}^{*}}\mathcal{F} satisfies σmin​(𝐉t)≥1\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{J}_{t})\geq 1 for all tt. Under this non-contractive assumption, the expected cumulative error eNb​a​s​ee_{N}^{base} is unrolled through the product of time-varying Jacobians:

‖𝔼⁡[eNbase]‖=‖∑t=1N(∏k=tN−1𝐉k)​𝔼​[ηt]‖≥∑t=1N(∏k=tN−1σmin​(𝐉k))​μ≥N​μ,\|\mathbb{E}[e_{N}^{\text{base}}]\|=\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(\prod_{k=t}^{N-1}\mathbf{J}_{k}\right)\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t}]\right\|\geq\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(\prod_{k=t}^{N-1}\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{J}_{k})\right)\mu\geq N\mu, (9)

where ∏k=tN−1𝐉k\prod_{k=t}^{N-1}\mathbf{J}_{k} represents the error transition from step tt to NN. Since the growth is at least linear in NN, the squared bias satisfies ‖𝔼⁡[eNbase]‖2=Ω⁡(N2)\|\mathbb{E}[e_{N}^{\text{base}}]\|^{2}=\Omega(N^{2}).

Variance Accumulation. Even in an idealized scenario where the generator is unbiased (𝔼⁡[ηt]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t}]=0), the AR process remains unstable due to stochastic noise accumulation. Modeling {ηt}\{\eta_{t}\} as i.i.d. random variables with variance Tr​(Cov​(ηt))=σ2\text{Tr}(\text{Cov}(\eta_{t}))=\sigma^{2}, the variance of the cumulative error is:

Tr​(Cov​(eNbase))=∑t=1NTr​(Cov​(ηt))=N​σ2.\text{Tr}(\text{Cov}(e_{N}^{\text{base}}))=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\text{Tr}(\text{Cov}(\eta_{t}))=N\sigma^{2}. (10)

Under the decomposition MSE=‖Bias‖2+Variance\text{MSE}=\|\text{Bias}\|^{2}+\text{Variance}, the Mean Squared Error is lower-bounded by Ω⁡(N)\Omega(N). Physically, this indicates that pure AR models lack a corrective mechanism; without global anchors, both systematic drift and stochastic noise force the trajectory to diverge irreversibly from the ground truth.

Part II: Error Bounding via Keyframe-Assisted Interpolation

In contrast to the recursive accumulation in pure AR models, our strategy partitions the sequence into segments SiS_{i} using sparse keyframes {Ki}\{K_{i}\} at interval TT. For any frame t=i​T+τt=iT+\tau where τ∈(0,T)\tau\in(0,T) is the temporal offset within segment SiS_{i}, the generation process is defined by a conditional interpolation mapping 𝒢\mathcal{G}:

Ii​T+τ=𝒢⁡(Ki,Ki+1,Si−1,τ,ϵτ),I_{iT+\tau}=\mathcal{G}(K_{i},K_{i+1},S_{i-1},\tau,\epsilon_{\tau}), (11)

where KiK_{i} and Ki+1K_{i+1} are the bidirectional global anchors, Si−1S_{i-1} provides the preceding temporal context (momentum), and ϵτ\epsilon_{\tau} represents the local sampling noise.

Step 1: Unified Decomposition Framework

For any frame t=i​T+τt=iT+\tau in segment SiS_{i} (τ∈(0,T)\tau\in(0,T)), we model the generation process as the superposition of two components: a Brownian Bridge BτB_{\tau} pinned at the keyframes {Ki,Ki+1}\{K_{i},K_{i+1}\} to ensure global structural alignment, and an autoregressive residual Φi​(τ)\Phi_{i}(\tau) to maintain temporal continuity from the preceding segment Si−1S_{i-1}. Specifically, Ii​T+τ=Bτ+Φi​(τ)I_{iT+\tau}=B_{\tau}+\Phi_{i}(\tau), where the Brownian Bridge BτB_{\tau} is a stochastic process characterized by:

𝔼⁡[Bτ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[B_{\tau}] =(1−τT)​Ki+τT​Ki+1,\displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{\tau}{T}\right)K_{i}+\frac{\tau}{T}K_{i+1}, (12)
Var​(Bτ)\displaystyle\text{Var}(B_{\tau}) =τ⁡(T−τ)T​σi​n​t2,\displaystyle=\frac{\tau(T-\tau)}{T}\sigma_{int}^{2}, (13)

where σi​n​t2\sigma_{int}^{2} denotes the interpolation noise intensity. Under this framework, the generated state Ii​T+τI_{iT+\tau} is the sum of the bridge mean, the cross-segment consistency shift Φi​(τ)\Phi_{i}(\tau) (representing momentum), and stochastic bridge noise ϵτ∼𝒩⁡(0,Var​(Bτ))\epsilon_{\tau}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\text{Var}(B_{\tau})).

Assuming the ground-truth trajectory It∗I_{t}^{*} follows a similar Brownian Bridge dynamic anchored at ground-truth keyframes {Ki∗}\{K_{i}^{*}\}, the interpolation error ei​T+τours=It−It∗e_{iT+\tau}^{\text{ours}}=I_{t}-I_{t}^{*} is derived by subtracting the respective components:

ei​T+τours=(1−τT)​e​(Ki)+τT​e​(Ki+1)⏟Ea​n​c​h​ (Boundary Interpolation)+δi​(τ)⏟El​e​a​k​ (Momentum Leakage)+wτ⏟En​o​i​s​e​ (Local Noise),\displaystyle e_{iT+\tau}^{\text{ours}}=\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{\tau}{T}\right)e(K_{i})+\frac{\tau}{T}e(K_{i+1})}_{E_{anch}\text{ (Boundary Interpolation)}}+\underbrace{\delta_{i}(\tau)}_{E_{leak}\text{ (Momentum Leakage)}}+\underbrace{w_{\tau}}_{E_{noise}\text{ (Local Noise)}}, (14)

where Ea​n​c​hE_{anch} results from the linear interpolation of keyframe drifts e⁡(Ki)=Ki−Ki∗e(K_{i})=K_{i}-K_{i}^{*}, El​e​a​k=Φ−Φ∗E_{leak}=\Phi-\Phi^{*} is the implicit autoregressive error (momentum leakage), and En​o​i​s​e=ϵ−ϵ∗E_{noise}=\epsilon-\epsilon^{*} is the local stochastic hallucination. To prove global stability, we must show that El​e​a​kE_{leak} remains bounded independently of the sequence length NN.

Step 2: Damping of Momentum Leakage

To maintain temporal continuity while adhering to fixed keyframes, the video model implicitly minimizes the acceleration along the error trajectory δi​(τ)\delta_{i}(\tau), where τ∈[0,T]\tau\in[0,T] is the frame offset. This corresponds to minimizing the second-order energy functional:

L⁡(δi)=∫0T(δi′′​(τ))2​𝑑τ.L(\delta_{i})=\int_{0}^{T}(\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}(\tau))^{2}d\tau. (15)

Under these dynamics, the momentum error entering from the preceding segment Si−1S_{i-1} is defined as Δ​vi−1=δi−1′​(T)\Delta v_{i-1}=\delta_{i-1}^{\prime}(T). This term acts as the initial velocity constraint δi′​(0)=Δ​vi−1\delta_{i}^{\prime}(0)=\Delta v_{i-1}, which is then structurally damped across the current segment.

Lemma 1 (Damping Coefficient)

The transmitted velocity error Δ​vi\Delta v_{i} at the boundary satisfies the recurrence Δ​vi=γ​Δ​vi−1\Delta v_{i}=\gamma\Delta v_{i-1}, where the damping factor is:

γ=−12.\gamma=-{1\over 2}. (16)
Proof

The Euler-Lagrange equation for a functional involving second-order derivatives, L=∫f⁡(τ,δi,δi′,δi′′)​𝑑τL=\int f(\tau,\delta_{i},\delta_{i}^{\prime},\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime})d\tau with f=(δi′′)2f=(\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime})^{2}, is given by:

∂f∂δi−dd​τ​(∂f∂δi′)+d2d​τ2​(∂f∂δi′′)=0.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\delta_{i}}-\frac{d}{d\tau}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\delta_{i}^{\prime}}\right)+\frac{d^{2}}{d\tau^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}}\right)=0. (17)

Since ff only depends on the second derivative δi′′\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}, we have ∂f∂δi=0\frac{\partial f}{\partial\delta_{i}}=0 and ∂f∂δi′=0\frac{\partial f}{\partial\delta_{i}^{\prime}}=0. Substituting ∂f∂δi′′=2​δi′′​(τ)\frac{\partial f}{\partial\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}}=2\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}(\tau) into the equation yields:

d2d​τ2​(2​δi′′​(τ))=0⟹2​δi(4)​(τ)=0\frac{d^{2}}{d\tau^{2}}(2\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}(\tau))=0\implies 2\delta_{i}^{(4)}(\tau)=0 (18)

Thus, the governing equation is δi(4)​(τ)=0\delta_{i}^{(4)}(\tau)=0. The general solution to this fourth-order linear differential equation is a cubic polynomial:

δi​(τ)=a​τ3+b​τ2+c​τ+d.\delta_{i}(\tau)=a\tau^{3}+b\tau^{2}+c\tau+d. (19)

To isolate the effect of velocity leakage, we apply the positional anchoring and smoothness constraints:

δi​(0)=0,δi​(T)=0\displaystyle\delta_{i}(0)=0,\quad\delta_{i}(T)=0 (Rigid Positional Anchors),\displaystyle\quad\text{(Rigid Positional Anchors)}, (20)
δi′​(0)=Δ​vi−1\displaystyle\delta_{i}^{\prime}(0)=\Delta v_{i-1} (Velocity Continuity),\displaystyle\quad\text{(Velocity Continuity)}, (21)
δi′′​(T)=0\displaystyle\delta_{i}^{\prime\prime}(T)=0  (Natural Boundary Condition). (22)

Substituting these conditions into the cubic form yields the following algebraic system:

d=0,c\displaystyle d=0,\quad c =Δ​vi−1,\displaystyle=\Delta v_{i-1}, (23)
6​a​T+2​b\displaystyle 6aT+2b =0⟹b=−3​a​T,\displaystyle=0\implies b=-3aT, (24)
a​T3+(−3​a​T)​T2+Δ​vi−1​T\displaystyle aT^{3}+(-3aT)T^{2}+\Delta v_{i-1}T =0⟹a=Δ​vi−12​T2.\displaystyle=0\implies a=\frac{\Delta v_{i-1}}{2T^{2}}. (25)

The velocity error transmitted to the start of the next segment Si+1S_{i+1} is the derivative at the current segment’s end τ=T\tau=T:

Δ​vi=δi′​(T)\displaystyle\Delta v_{i}=\delta_{i}^{\prime}(T) =3​a​T2+2​b​T+c\displaystyle=3aT^{2}+2bT+c
=3​(Δ​vi−12​T2)​T2+2​(−3​Δ​vi−12​T)​T+Δ​vi−1\displaystyle=3\left(\frac{\Delta v_{i-1}}{2T^{2}}\right)T^{2}+2\left(-\frac{3\Delta v_{i-1}}{2T}\right)T+\Delta v_{i-1}

The geometric progression |γ|=0.5<1|\gamma|=0.5<1 confirms that the momentum error is exponentially attenuated across segments, ensuring that the system remains globally stable and avoids the cumulative divergence typical of pure AR models.

Furthermore, we analyze the maximum magnitude of the leakage term ‖δi​(τ)‖\|\delta_{i}(\tau)\| within a single segment to bound the local drift. By identifying the extremum where δi′​(τ)=0\delta_{i}^{\prime}(\tau)=0 (occurring at τ∗=T⁡(1−33)\tau^{*}=T(1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})), the intra-segment peak error is given by:

maxτ∈[0,T]⁡‖δi​(τ)‖=39​T​‖Δ​vi−1‖≈0.192​T​‖Δ​vi−1‖.\max_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|\delta_{i}(\tau)\|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}T\|\Delta v_{i-1}\|\approx 0.192T\|\Delta v_{i-1}\|. (27)

This result shows that the momentum leakage is locally constrained by the keyframe interval TT and remains strictly proportional to the incoming velocity error, providing a theoretical guarantee for the unified global bound.

Step 3: Synthesis of the Unified Global Bound

Substituting the results from the previous steps into the decomposition framework of Eq. 14, we synthesize the final upper bound for the generation error. By the triangle inequality, the total error norm is bounded by the sum of three distinct components:

‖ei​T+τours‖≤‖Ea​n​c​h‖⏟Keyframe Drift+‖El​e​a​k‖⏟Momentum Leakage+‖En​o​i​s​e‖⏟Interpolation Variance.\|e_{iT+\tau}^{\text{ours}}\|\leq\underbrace{\|E_{anch}\|}_{\text{Keyframe Drift}}+\underbrace{\|E_{leak}\|}_{\text{Momentum Leakage}}+\underbrace{\|E_{noise}\|}_{\text{Interpolation Variance}}. (28)

We analyze each component to establish the global stability:

  • •

    Keyframe Drift (‖Ea​n​c​h‖\|E_{anch}\|): This term depends on the strategy used to generate {Kj}\{K_{j}\}.

    1. 1.

      Global Generation: If keyframes are generated globally (e.g., via a sparse pre-selected set), ‖e⁡(Kj)‖≤Ck​f\|e(K_{j})\|\leq C_{kf}, yielding ‖Ea​n​c​h‖=𝒪⁡(1)\|E_{anch}\|=\mathcal{O}(1).

    2. 2.

      Downsampled AR: If keyframes are generated autoregressively with step TT, the error accumulates over N/TN/T steps. Following Part I, ‖e⁡(Kj)‖=𝒪⁡(N/T)\|e(K_{j})\|=\mathcal{O}(N/T), which represents a TT-fold suppression of the pure AR drift 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N).

  • •

    Momentum Leakage (‖El​e​a​k‖\|E_{leak}\|): From Lemma 1, the velocity error satisfies Δ​vi=γ​Δ​vi−1\Delta v_{i}=\gamma\Delta v_{i-1} with |γ|=0.5|\gamma|=0.5. The cumulative velocity error is bounded by the geometric series ∑k=0iγk​‖Δ​v0‖≤2​‖Δ​v0‖\sum_{k=0}^{i}\gamma^{k}\|\Delta v_{0}\|\leq 2\|\Delta v_{0}\|. Combined with the intra-segment peak derived in Step 2:

    supi,τ‖δi​(τ)‖≤0.192​T⋅(2​‖Δ​v0‖)=0.384​T​‖Δ​v0‖.\sup_{i,\tau}\|\delta_{i}(\tau)\|\leq 0.192T\cdot(2\|\Delta v_{0}\|)=0.384T\|\Delta v_{0}\|. (29)

    Crucially, this term is only dependent of the keyframe interval (T)(T) and independent of the total sequence length NN, confirming that momentum error does not diverge.

  • •

    Interpolation Variance (‖En​o​i​s​e‖\|E_{noise}\|): The local stochastic error is governed by the Brownian Bridge variance Var​(Bτ)=τ⁡(T−τ)T​σi​n​t2\text{Var}(B_{\tau})=\frac{\tau(T-\tau)}{T}\sigma_{int}^{2}. To find the upper bound, we maximize this quadratic form with respect to τ\tau:

    dd​τ​(τ​T−τ2T)=0⟹τ=T2;maxτ⁡Var​(Bτ)=T4​σi​n​t2.\frac{d}{d\tau}\left(\frac{\tau T-\tau^{2}}{T}\right)=0\implies\tau=\frac{T}{2};\quad\max_{\tau}\text{Var}(B_{\tau})=\frac{T}{4}\sigma_{int}^{2}. (30)

    Thus, ‖En​o​i​s​e‖≤T2​σi​n​t\|E_{noise}\|\leq\frac{\sqrt{T}}{2}\sigma_{int}, indicating that local hallucination is strictly constrained by the segment length.

Conclusion: Combining these results, the unified global bound is:

‖etours‖≤maxj⁡‖e⁡(Kj)‖+0.384​T|Δ​v0|+T2​σi​n​t.\|e_{t}^{\text{ours}}\|\leq\max_{j}\|e(K_{j})\|+0.384T\|\Delta v_{0}\|+\frac{\sqrt{T}}{2}\sigma_{int}. (31)

Unlike the Ω⁡(N)\Omega(N) divergence of pure AR models, our method ensures that the error is dominated by the quality of sparse keyframes and the local segment length TT. Even in the worst-case AR keyframe scenario, the MSE is suppressed by a factor of T2T^{2}, effectively neutralizing catastrophic temporal decay and establishing long-term generation stability.

Conclusion on Keyframe Scenarios: If keyframes are generated globally, ‖etours‖=𝒪⁡(1)\|e_{t}^{\text{ours}}\|=\mathcal{O}(1). If keyframes are generated autoregressively with step TT, ‖etours‖=𝒪⁡(N/T)\|e_{t}^{\text{ours}}\|=\mathcal{O}(N/T), achieving a TT-fold (and T2T^{2} in MSE) suppression of degradation compared to pure AR. The theoretical results establish the advantage of our method over pure AR generation, and the subsequent experimental results further confirm this advantage empirically.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Training Details

Interpolation Stage Training. For the training of the interpolation generator GIG_{I}, we employ a stochastic keyframe conditioning strategy to enhance the model’s robustness to diverse temporal contexts. Specifically, for each training segment, we randomly sample 11 to 1010 conditioning keyframes from the keyframe set 𝒦\mathcal{K}. These keyframes are restricted to a temporal window within ±10\pm 10 frames of the target segment’s range to simulate local structural anchors. Furthermore, to facilitate the Motion-Inductive Noisy Conditioning (Sec. 4.3), the guidance coefficient αc\alpha_{c} is randomly sampled from the range [0.1,0.5][0.1,0.5] during training, ensuring that the model learns to prioritize underlying motion dynamics over simple pixel-level replication.

Baseline Implementation. To ensure a fair and comprehensive comparison, we evaluate our model against several state-of-the-art baselines. For consistency, all compared models are provided with camera trajectories as conditional inputs. We independently implemented the training and inference pipelines for SEVA [36] and Diffusion Forcing [3] following the architectures described in their respective papers. For other baseline methods, we utilized their official open-source repositories and strictly adhered to the recommended training configurations and hyperparameters. All models, including our re-implementations, were trained until convergence to ensure they reached their optimal performance levels for the benchmarking tasks.

Evaluation Metrics and Resolutions. We report the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) to assess visual quality and temporal consistency. For FID calculations, while SEVA uses its default 299×299299\times 299 resolution (aligned with the standard Inception-v3 input), all other methods, including our own, are evaluated at a resolution of 256×448256\times 448 to match the native aspect ratio of the datasets. For the FVD metric, all compared methods are evaluated at a unified resolution of 224×224224\times 224 using the standard I3D backbone to ensure a consistent and unbiased comparison of temporal dynamics.

Appendix C Additional Results

This section provides supplementary qualitative evidence to further substantiate our experimental findings and theoretical analysis.

C.1 Extended Comparisons in Long-Trajectory Generation

We present additional visual comparisons to further demonstrate the superiority of the DCARL framework in long-term video synthesis. As illustrated in Fig. A and Fig. B, our method maintains significantly higher temporal consistency and trajectory fidelity over extended horizons compared to existing baselines. While competing methods often suffer from visual drifting or structural collapse as the sequence progresses, DCARL leverages sparse keyframe anchors to ensure stable and realistic scene evolution throughout the entire trajectory.

C.2 Comparisons in Small-Scene Generation

To further evaluate the generalization capability of DCARL, we conduct experiments on the DL3DV-10K dataset [16], which focuses on detailed small-scene reconstruction and generation. The quantitative results are summarized in Tab. A.

As illustrated in Fig. C, our method significantly outperforms autoregressive baselines in maintaining long-term visual stability and trajectory adherence. We observe that while existing AR methods often suffer from cumulative exposure bias—leading to gradual semantic drift or visual degradation over extended sequences—DCARL effectively eliminates such artifacts, preserving consistent scene appearance throughout the rollout. Furthermore, our model exhibits superior alignment with the input camera trajectories. While baseline methods frequently deviate from the intended path or exhibit trajectory drift during complex maneuvers, DCARL’s keyframe-anchored strategy ensures that the generated views remain strictly faithful to the provided motion constraints, ensuring high-fidelity controllable generation.

C.3 Failure Cases

Despite the robust performance of DCARL, we identify certain scenarios where the model still faces challenges, as illustrated in Fig. D. These failure cases provide insights into current limitations and future research directions.

Long-distance Perception Limits. The first and second rows of Fig. D demonstrate that there is still room for improvement in long-range spatial perception. In the first row, the model fails to correctly anchor the vegetation, which should ideally remain within the center of the roundabout. In the second row, the generated trajectory incorrectly passes through a pedestrian island, indicating a lack of fine-grained understanding of complex road boundaries over long distances.

Corner Cases and Data Distribution. The third row depicts a challenging corner case where the sequence originates from beneath an overpass. Upon exiting the overpass, the model produces unrealistic and unnatural visual artifacts. Such failures suggest that the model remains sensitive to rare structural transitions and lighting changes.

These observations highlight the necessity of designing more sophisticated long-distance perception mechanisms and further enriching the training set with a more balanced and diverse distribution of corner cases.

Appendix D Discussion

While DCARL effectively addresses the cumulative divergence in long-term video synthesis, we acknowledge several limitations that provide avenues for future research.

Real-time Generation. Although DCARL does not introduce significantly more inference latency compared to standard bidirectional attention-based models, it is not yet optimized for real-time interactive applications. However, our framework offers a promising blueprint for real-time streaming synthesis. Specifically, future iterations could employ a dual-stream architecture: a high-speed causal model could handle low-latency frame generation, while a secondary sparse model generates and maintains a global scene representation—either as a collection of memory frames or 3D primitives—to provide structural anchors. Our work demonstrates that this divide-and-conquer approach is instrumental in stabilizing such real-time autoregressive processes.

Keyframe Generation Quality. Currently, the generation quality of sparse keyframes is slightly constrained by the inherent difficulty of learning long-range data distributions compared to short-window transitions. This challenge manifests in maintaining high-frequency visual details and precise camera trajectory adherence over ultra-long horizons. Under limited computational and data resources, we believe the dual-generator design remains optimal, and the keyframe generator could be further enhanced by distilling knowledge from 3D foundation models. While a unified generator representation might potentially yield higher quality, it would require significantly larger compute budgets and more diverse data representations. At present, DCARL ensures robust 32-second video generation with high-fidelity camera control and visual stability.
